title: Writing with iron-gall ink
subtitle: Using the traditional manuscript ink that writes pale and darkens on the page
excerpt: Iron-gall ink writes a grey-green colour and darkens to a rich brown-black on the page as the iron oxidises. It flows freely from broad-edge nibs, bites into paper slightly, and is water-resistant once dry. The behaviour differs enough from carbon and sumi inks to be worth understanding before using it on finished work.
sourceNotes: Edward Johnston, Writing and Illuminating and Lettering (1906), chapter on inks: description of iron-gall ink preparation and its behaviour on vellum and on sized paper. The history of iron-gall ink in European manuscript production is well documented in conservation literature; this entry draws on Johnston's practical observations.

glossaryTerms.definition: An ink made from tannins (from oak galls or similar) combined with iron sulphate. The ink is initially pale and acidic; the iron oxidises on exposure to air, darkening the colour to a warm brown-black over minutes to hours.
Historic iron-gall inks were highly acidic and ate through manuscript pages over centuries. Modern buffered formulations are designed to minimise this risk, but long-term testing is still ongoing.

items.name: Iron-gall ink, modern buffered formulation
items.notes: Several brands produce a pH-neutral or mildly buffered iron-gall. The Registrar's iron-gall is one of the best known for calligraphy. Avoid vintage corrosive formulations on work you want to keep long-term.

items.name: Mitchell Roundhand nib, 3 (medium)
items.notes: Iron-gall flows readily from broad-edge nibs. Rinse the nib after every session: the iron particles can clog fine reservoirs if left to dry.

items.name: Cartridge paper, 220 gsm, for finished work
items.notes: Iron-gall ink bites slightly into unsized papers; on lightweight cartridge it can feather. Heavier paper or alum-sized paper gives cleaner lines.

items.name: Cartridge paper, 130 gsm, for practice
items.notes: Fine for practice sheets even if some feathering occurs.

content.text: Dip the nib to the vent hole only. Iron-gall ink is thinner than most commercial calligraphy inks, so the reservoir does not hold as much. Write four to six letters before the next dip. Wipe the underside of the nib on the bottle rim to remove the excess drop that would otherwise blob at the first touch of the paper.

The ink writes as a grey-green or blue-grey depending on the formulation. On paper the colour darkens to brown-black within 10 to 30 minutes as the iron oxidises. This means that freshly written text looks lighter than the final result. Do not add more ink to a thin-looking passage while the writing is wet: the line will almost certainly darken to a good density once dry. On sized paper the oxidation is slightly faster than on unsized cartridge.

Rinse nibs immediately after each session. Iron-gall ink contains iron particles that bond to the metal surface and cause surface rust within a day if left to dry. Rinse by dipping in clean water, wiping dry on a lint-free cloth, and storing in a dry container. Mitchell nibs last years with this care; neglected, they rust visibly within a week and lose their edge.

items.symptom: The ink skips and flows unevenly from the nib
items.cause: The nib surface has a lacquer coating from manufacture. Iron-gall ink will not adhere until this is removed.
items.fix: Pass the nib through a flame briefly (two seconds maximum) or wipe it with isopropyl alcohol on a cotton swab. Re-dip and test.

items.symptom: The ink feathers badly on the paper
items.cause: The paper is too absorbent for iron-gall ink. Very lightweight or uncoated newsprint-style papers are not suitable.
items.fix: Move to 130 gsm cartridge or heavier. Alternatively, size the paper with a light coat of diluted PVA, allowed to dry, before writing.
